title: The opening line (incipit)
greek: sa naqba imuru (SB); sutur eli sarri (Old Babylonian)
short: Thompson's first line praises a man who has 'proven all matters'; George's text reads 'He who saw the Deep', which was also the ancient title of the epic.
body: Babylonian poems were named by their first words, and the standard version was catalogued as 'He who saw the Deep' (sa naqba imuru). Thompson's rendering reflects the older understanding of naqbu as 'totality', hence 'He who (the heart of) all matters hath proven'. George (2003) argues that naqbu here means the Deep, the subterranean waters of the god Ea, so that the line already points to the hero's journey to the edge of the world and to the wisdom of Uta-Napishtim, who survived the Flood sent from those waters. Both senses are probably in play. The older Old Babylonian version began differently, 'Surpassing all kings' (sutur eli sarri). The opening is a hymn of praise in the third person: the poem presents Gilgamish as a sage who learned through suffering, not only as a warrior. Note that Thompson marks his own supplements with round brackets and restorations with square ones; the lines are badly broken here.

title: Knowledge 'from before the Flood'
short: Gilgamish brings back an account of the time before the Flood: the prologue already announces Uta-Napishtim's story in Tablet XI.
body: Thompson's 'handed down the tradition relating to (things) prediluvian' renders a line which George translates as bringing back 'a message from before the Flood'. In Mesopotamian thought the antediluvian age was the time of the Seven Sages (apkallu), who taught mankind the arts of civilisation; knowledge 'from before the Flood' was the most authoritative knowledge there was. The prologue therefore tells the reader where the story will end: at the house of the Flood hero (Tablet XI). The sequence of the prologue (wisdom, a journey, weariness, a written record) summarises the whole poem in advance, a technique of anticipation that the epic uses again in its closing return to the walls of Uruk.

title: The 'table of stone': the hero's written record
short: Gilgamish sets down his labours on a stone monument: the poem presents itself as the text of that inscription.
body: The Akkadian word is naru, a stone stele of the kind kings erected to record their deeds. After Thompson's time further manuscripts restored the rest of the prologue (George I.24-28): the reader is told to find a box of cedar, open its bronze clasp and take out a tablet of lapis lazuli on which Gilgamish's hardships are written. The epic thus claims to be the hero's own memorial, which the reader is invited to 'read aloud'. This frame turns the poem into a reflection on writing and fame: Gilgamish fails to win eternal life, but his name survives in a text. Thompson's translation lacks the box passage because it was not yet known, so his prologue breaks off before the reader is addressed directly.

title: Erech (Uruk) 'the high-walled'
short: Erech is the Biblical name of Uruk (modern Warka), Gilgamish's city; Thompson's 'high-wall'd' renders an epithet George reads as 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold'.
body: Uruk, on an old course of the Euphrates in southern Iraq, was one of the first true cities of the world, and Genesis 10:10 names it 'Erech' among the cities of Nimrod; Thompson uses that Biblical form throughout. The standard epithet Uruk supuri was long understood as 'Uruk of the enclosure', hence Thompson's 'high-wall'd'. George translates 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold', which fits the image of the king as 'shepherd' of his people (see 'shepherd of Erech' below), though the enclosing walls are still implied. The walls themselves were famous: later tradition credited Gilgamish with building them, and the poem ends where it begins, with the invitation to walk on them (XI). In the Old Babylonian tablets the city is instead 'Uruk of the broad squares' (Thompson's 'broad-marketed', Tablet II).

title: E-Anna, temple of Anu and Ishtar
short: E-Anna, 'House of Heaven', was the great temple precinct of Uruk, sacred to the sky-god Anu and to Ishtar.
body: Thompson's note explains E-Anna as the great temple of Anu and Ishtar, where Ishtar's cult was served by temple women, a point that matters for the courtesan who will civilise Enkidu. Excavations at Warka have uncovered the Eanna precinct, one of the oldest monumental temple complexes known. Thompson's 'treasury hallow'd' reflects his understanding of the temple as a store of sacred wealth. The prologue praises Gilgamish as builder: Mesopotamian kings boasted above all of building walls and temples, and the poem places its hero in that tradition before telling of his oppression of the city. Ishtar herself appears in person in Tablet VI, and her cult personnel (devotees and courtesans) mourn the Bull of Heaven there.

title: Two-thirds god, one-third man
short: Gilgamish is two-thirds divine and one-third human: the arithmetic is odd, but the point is that his human third makes him mortal.
body: The son of the goddess Nin-sun and of Lugal-banda (a deified king), Gilgamish is described as two parts god and one part man, a formula restored by Thompson from the Ninth Tablet, where the scorpion-man's wife repeats it. How the proportion arises is never explained, and scholars have proposed various explanations; the essential point is that he is more than human but less than divine. The phrasing is crucial to the plot: however great his strength, the human part is enough to subject him to death. The epic keeps reminding us of this tension, through his superhuman energy (he is 'restless' day and night) and through his failure in Tablet XI to stay awake for even a week. The historical Gilgamesh, king of Uruk in the early third millennium BC, was worshipped after death as a judge in the underworld.

title: 'Like an aurochs': the wild bull
short: The aurochs (rimu), the huge wild bull of the Near East, is the epic's standard image for Gilgamish's overwhelming strength.
body: The wild bull was a royal image in Mesopotamia: kings are 'wild bulls' in inscriptions, and Gilgamish's mother Nin-sun is herself a 'wild cow' (see Tablet II). The image is double-edged here: the bull's towering crest and unmatched weapons are the complaint of the oppressed citizens, who repeat it to the gods. The heroes later fight 'like bulls' (II) and kill the Bull of Heaven (VI), so bovine imagery runs through the poem. The aurochs (Bos primigenius) is now extinct, which is why Thompson uses the old name rather than 'buffalo' or 'bison'. The repetition of the people's complaint word for word in the gods' report to Anu is typical of Akkadian narrative style.

title: The tyranny of Gilgamish
short: The citizens complain that Gilgamish takes sons from fathers and girls from mothers: the nature of the oppression is left unclear.
body: The young men are 'driven into the toils' (Thompson's note: captured), perhaps exhausted in forced labour on the walls or in endless athletic contests, while young women are taken from their families. Scholars disagree about what is meant. George notes that the text never states the exact abuse; the Old Babylonian Tablet II makes clear that the king claimed the right to sleep with brides before their husbands (see 'woman allotted by fate'), which may be part of the complaint. The repeated lament (spoken by the people, then by the gods to Anu) frames the problem the plot will solve: the gods do not punish Gilgamish but create an equal to absorb his energy. Kingship in the poem is power without a peer, and the cure is friendship.

title: 'Shepherd of Erech': the king as shepherd
short: 'Shepherd' (re'u) is the ordinary Mesopotamian title of a king, who should protect his flock: here it is spoken with bitter irony.
body: From Sumerian times kings called themselves shepherds of their people; Hammurabi's law-code opens with the claim that he is the shepherd chosen by Enlil. When the citizens say 'he is the shepherd of Erech' while describing how he preys on them, the title becomes an indictment. The image may also lie behind the city's epithet Uruk supuri, 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold', as George reads it. The pastoral motif recurs when Enkidu becomes a watchman for real shepherds in Tablet II, protecting their flocks from lions, and when Ishtar's lover the Shepherd is turned into a beast in Tablet VI. Compare the Biblical shepherd-king David and the Homeric 'shepherd of the people' (poimen laon).

title: Anu, god of heaven
short: Anu is the sky-god, head of the pantheon and patron of Uruk; Thompson's 'Seigneur of Erech' renders his title as lord of the city.
body: An/Anu was the father of the gods, remote in his heaven but the ultimate source of kingship and authority. His temple was the E-Anna at Uruk, which he shared with Ishtar, here called his daughter (VI). The gods turn to Anu first because Gilgamish is 'his' king; Anu in turn commissions Aruru. Thompson's French 'Seigneur' is one of several medievalising touches in his version. Anu's role in the plot is that of a cautious elder: he grants Ishtar the Bull of Heaven only after warning of famine (VI), and he presides at the council that dooms Enkidu (VII).

title: Aruru, the mother-goddess
short: Aruru is a name of the mother-goddess who created mankind; Anu asks her to make Gilgamish's match.
body: Thompson's note calls Aruru a form of Nin-makh, 'especially as protectress of children'. She is one of several names of the birth goddess (also Belet-ili, Nintu, Mami). Her method echoes the creation of humans: she washes her hands, pinches off clay and casts it 'on the desert'. In the Atrahasis epic the mother-goddess Mami likewise shapes the first humans from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of a slain god; Genesis 2:7 has God form man 'of the dust of the ground'. Enkidu is thus a new first man, made outside the city, who must be brought step by step into civilisation. Her task is literally to make a 'double' (zikru, an image or counterpart) of Gilgamish: the theme of the second self begins here.

title: Enkidu, the wild man
short: Enkidu is the wild man created as Gilgamish's equal: hairy, naked, living with the gazelles until he is drawn into human society.
body: The name is Sumerian; its meaning is uncertain (often explained as 'Lord of the pleasant place'). Older scholars read it 'Ea-bani', a reading Jastrow and Clay (1920) declared must be 'definitely abandoned' on the evidence of the Old Babylonian spelling. Enkidu's long hair 'like a woman's', his life among the animals, and his freeing of the trapper's prey make him the opposite of the city king. In Sumerian poems Enkidu is Gilgamesh's servant; the Akkadian epic makes him a friend and equal, which Tigay identifies as one of the main innovations of the Old Babylonian poet. His humanisation, in stages (sex, bread and beer, clothing, shepherd's work, the city), offers a Mesopotamian account of what it means to be human.

title: Ninurta
short: Ninurta is the warrior son of Enlil, god of war and the hunt; Enkidu is made strong as if by his hand.
body: Thompson's note: 'A god, son of Enlil, patron of war and hunting.' His rendering 'of Ninurta the double' reflects one reading of a difficult phrase; George understands kisir Ninurta as 'knit strong by Ninurta' (literally, 'a knot' or 'concentration' of Ninurta), i.e. endowed with the god's compact strength. Either way Enkidu's power is linked to the god who in myth defeated monsters of the mountains, appropriate for a creature born in the wild hills. Ninurta reappears in the Flood story (XI) as the gods' 'herald' and as a bringer of havoc in the storm. He was worshipped above all at Nippur, beside his father Enlil.

title: Sumuqan (Shakkan), god of the herds
short: Sumuqan is the god of cattle and wild animals; dressed 'like Sumuqan', Enkidu is naked or clad in skins like the beasts.
body: Thompson's note: 'God of cattle and agriculture.' Modern editors read the name as Shakkan (Sumuqan is the older reading of the same signs). He was the patron of the herds and wild animals of the steppe, and the phrase means that Enkidu wears what the animals wear, either nothing or hides. The phrase is ironic once Enkidu is clothed by the courtesan in Tablet II. Shakkan appears again among the dead in Enkidu's dream of the underworld (VII), where Thompson keeps the form 'Sumuqan'.

title: The courtesan (Shamhat)
short: The woman who civilises Enkidu is a courtesan (harimtu); modern editions call her Shamhat, a name Thompson does not use.
body: Thompson renders harimtu with the Greek 'hetaera', and later calls her 'the nymph' and 'doxy' (II), all classicising or archaic words. Modern editions (George 2003) read her personal name as Shamhat, 'the voluptuous one', a name related to samhatu, one of the classes of Ishtar's women listed in Tablet VI. Whether such women were cult personnel ('sacred prostitutes') or simply prostitutes of the city is debated; many recent scholars are sceptical of the older notion of sacred prostitution. Her role is positive and civilising: she gives Enkidu sexual experience, then food, clothing and speech, and leads him to Uruk. Enkidu later curses her and then, rebuked by Shamash, blesses her (VII).

title: 'Six days, seven nights'
short: Enkidu lies with the woman 'six days, seven nights': a formulaic span used at key moments throughout the poem.
body: The count of six and seven marks completion in Akkadian poetry. It recurs for the Flood's storm (XI: six days and seven nights), for Uta-Napishtim's challenge to stay awake 'six days and seven nights' (XI), and for Gilgamish's mourning over Enkidu until a worm drops from his corpse (X). The repetition binds the poem's three thresholds together: entry into human life, the ending of human life, and the failed attempt to escape death. Compare Genesis 1-2, where creation is completed in six days with rest on the seventh.

title: Enkidu's 'loss of innocence'
short: After his week with the woman, the animals flee from Enkidu; he has lost his bond with the wild but gained understanding.
body: Thompson's note offers alternatives for the phrase ('the innocence of his body' or 'the excellence of his bodily strength'), and he compares the belief, widespread in the East since Adam and Eve, that sexual knowledge ends a state of innocence. The parallel with Genesis 2-3 is often drawn: a man made from earth gains knowledge through a woman, his eyes are opened, and he must leave his first state. George and others caution that the Babylonian story is not about sin: Enkidu's change is presented as growth ('he hath broaden'd (his) wisdom'), and the woman's next words praise him as 'like a god'. The episode is the first stage of a gradual humanisation completed in Tablet II.

title: Ishtar
short: Ishtar, goddess of sexual love and of war, is the patron goddess of Uruk; she later proposes marriage to Gilgamish (VI).
body: Ishtar (Sumerian Inanna) was the most important goddess of Mesopotamia, associated with the planet Venus, with desire and fertility, and with battle. At Uruk she shared the E-Anna temple with Anu. Her servants included women whose sexuality was devoted to her, which is why the courtesan leads Enkidu to her 'dwelling'. The epic treats her with striking irreverence: in Tablet VI Gilgamish lists her ruined lovers, and in the Flood story (XI) she wails like a woman in childbirth over the destruction she has helped decree. Her 'Wailing' for Tammuz connects her with the annual lament for the dying god.

title: Uruk the festive city
short: The courtesan lures Enkidu with a picture of Uruk's festivals, music and temple women: the city is the place of pleasure as well as of power.
body: Thompson warns that the text here is mutilated and his rendering of two lines may not be exact. In George's edition the passage describes Uruk 'where every day is a festival', with drums, and with temple women (the courtesans of Ishtar) noted for their charms. The eunuch-priests and dancers Thompson restores belong to the cult of Ishtar, whose personnel included cross-dressing performers (kurgarru, assinnu). The city here is defined by pleasure, community and abundance, the opposite of the lonely steppe. Siduri's later advice (X) to fill one's belly, wear clean clothes and delight in wife and child returns to this ideal.

title: Shamash, the Sun-god
short: Shamash, the Sun-god and god of justice, is Gilgamish's protector throughout the Cedar Forest adventure and beyond.
body: Shamash sees everything as he crosses the sky, and therefore was the god of justice and of divination. In the epic he sponsors the expedition against Humbaba, sends the winds that pin the ogre down (V), defends the courtesan against Enkidu's curse (VII), and is the only being who crosses the ocean to the land of Uta-Napishtim (X). His wife is Aa (Aya). Gilgamish's prayers to him (III, IX) show the personal piety of the hero. The sun's daily journey from the eastern to the western mountains also gives the shape of Gilgamish's own journey through the tunnel of Mashu.

title: Enlil (and Ea)
short: Enlil, lord of the earth and executive of the gods, and Ea, god of the fresh waters and of wisdom, are with Anu the great triad of the pantheon.
body: Thompson glosses Enlil as 'The god Bel' and Ea as 'The god of the great waters'. Enlil, whose temple Ekur stood at Nippur, confers kingship and appoints Humbaba as guardian of the Cedar Forest (III), which is why he demands Enkidu's death (VII) and why he sends the Flood (XI). Ea (Sumerian Enki), who lives in the Apsu, the subterranean ocean, is the clever friend of mankind: he betrays the gods' plan to Uta-Napishtim (XI) and later allows Enkidu's ghost to rise (XII). The contrast between harsh Enlil and wily, merciful Ea runs through Mesopotamian myth.

title: Gilgamish's first dream: the meteor
short: Gilgamish dreams that something 'like Anu's own self' falls from the stars; his mother reads it as the coming of a friend.
body: This is the first of many dreams in the epic, each needing interpretation. The object that falls from the sky is, in George's reading, a kisru sa Anim, 'a lump of Anu', i.e. a meteorite. Thompson, working before this reading was established, translates 'something like unto Anu's own self'. The detail that Gilgamish 'like a woman' embraced it (also in the axe dream) has given rise to a debate: some read it as evidence of an erotic relationship between the heroes; others stress that the poem uses the language of marriage for intense friendship; George discusses the wordplay that underlies these images. The dream shows the people crowding round the object, kissing its feet: Enkidu will be honoured in Uruk.

title: Nin-sun 'who knoweth all wisdom'
short: Gilgamish's mother Nin-sun is the dream-interpreter of the epic, called 'clever, wise, knowing everything'.
body: Thompson's note asks whether the name of Nin-sun, Gilgamish's mother, should be restored in the break. Her epithet ('wise, versed in all knowledge' in George's version) introduces her role: she reads dreams correctly, which in Mesopotamia was a specialist skill. Throughout Tablets I-III she is the hero's adviser and intercessor with Shamash. Her interpretations here are reliable; contrast the reassuring but sometimes forced interpretations Enkidu gives of the ominous dreams on the road to the Forest (IV-V).

title: The second dream: the axe
short: In the second dream an axe falls on Erech; Nin-sun explains that the axe is a man, a friend who will never abandon him.
body: The doubling of dreams, each told and then explained, is typical of the epic's style. George (2003), following earlier scholars, points to puns: the words for 'lump' (kisru) and 'axe' (hassinnu) echo terms for cult personnel of Ishtar (kezru, assinnu), men whose sexual identity was ambiguous. The puns support, without settling, the debate about the sexual dimension of the friendship. Thompson's note on the dream passage only records textual difficulties. The axe also anticipates the weapons the heroes will forge for the Cedar Forest (III) and the axe Gilgamish carries on his journey (X).
